what_it_does: High-level synthesis (HLS) is a tool that automatically converts a high-level program (written in C or a similar language) into a circuit blueprint (a description of actual hardware logic on a chip or FPGA — a reconfigurable chip). Dynamic HLS generates 'dataflow' circuits where data flows between operations through handshake signals (each unit tells the next 'I have data ready' / 'I am ready to receive'), and every operation gets its own dedicated hardware unit, which wastes area when several operations could take turns sharing a single unit. Sharing hardware units sounds simple but is actually dangerous in handshake-based circuits: if two operations both try to send data to a shared unit at the same time, and neither can make progress until the other finishes, the circuit can deadlock — freeze forever. CRUSH solves this by attaching a 'credit counter' to each shared unit: the counter tracks how many operations the unit can still accept; an operation may only proceed when it can obtain a credit (a permission token), and the credit is returned once the unit finishes that operation. This credit-based backpressure propagates through the handshake network to guarantee the unit is never overloaded, eliminating deadlock while enabling real hardware area savings.
